title: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties
goal: By the end you can predict what `by` forwards and to which object, read the fields the compiler generates for a delegated property, say what `by lazy` costs, and write your own delegate with `provideDelegate` validation.

warmup.q: `class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy`. You build it with `FlatFee(25)`, then set `fees.policy = FlatFee(99)`. What does `fees.feeMinor(10_000)` return?
options: 99, because `by policy` forwards to the property
25, because the delegate was captured when the object was built
It doesn't compile: a `var` can't be a delegate
It throws, because the delegate changed under it
warmup.why: The compiler copies the constructor argument into a hidden `private final FeePolicy $$delegate_0` field, and the generated `feeMinor` calls that field. Assigning `policy` changes the property only. It compiles without a warning, which is why the first option catches people.

analogy: A delegated property is a flat with a building manager. You own the flat, but every request to get in or change something goes through the manager, who can keep a log, refuse a change, or fetch the keys only on the first visit. Visitors from outside (Java callers) see an ordinary front door, a getter and a setter. The analogy breaks at class delegation: there the manager is fixed on the day the building opens, and changing the name on the mailbox (the `var`) doesn't change who answers.
in_your_world: Audit trails are the obvious fit in payments: a `PaymentDraft` whose `status` and `amountMinor` record every change for the compliance log, written once as a delegate instead of in every setter. Quarkus configuration usually arrives through `@ConfigMapping` interfaces, but code that reads a parsed `Map` (a merchant's routing rules from a JSON column, Kafka headers) can use map-backed properties, with `provideDelegate` to check the required keys when the object is built rather than on the first payment that needs them. And be careful with `by` on CDI beans: a bean that delegates an interface to a constructor argument keeps that argument forever. That's fine for an injected client, and wrong for anything you meant to swap at run time, such as a fee policy behind a feature flag.

compare.title: An audited field: Java setters vs a Kotlin delegate

java.title: PaymentDraft.java

kotlin.title: PaymentDraft.kt

compare.note: In Java the audit lives in every setter, and a new field without it is a silent gap that only review can catch. In Kotlin it's written once, in the delegate, and each property opts in with `by`. The property name comes from the `KProperty` the compiler passes in, so it can't drift from the field name the way a string literal can. The run-time price is one delegate object per property per instance, plus one static `KProperty` array per class. Java code calling the Kotlin class can't tell the two apart: it sees `getStatus` and `setStatus` either way.

worked.title: A config object that fails at startup, not on the first payment

steps.say: Start with a map-backed config. It reads nicely, but a missing key is found only when someone reads the property, which may be the first payment routed to that acquirer at 2 a.m.
Write a provider. `provideDelegate` runs once per property while the object is built, so it can check the key right away and hand back a delegate that only returns the value it read.
Build one with a key missing. It fails in the constructor, with the property's name in the message, because the name came from the `KProperty` the compiler passed in.

The cast is still unchecked: a `"timeoutMs" to "2000"` entry passes the check and fails later with a `ClassCastException` on the first read. If that matters, pass the expected class into `required` and check it with `isInstance`, the class-token trick from the generics track.

drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `class Clamped(min: Int, max: Int, initial: Int)` as a `ReadWriteProperty<Any?, Int>` that keeps every assigned value inside `min..max`, and use it as `var discountBps: Int by Clamped(0, 10_000, initial = 0)`. Then write the Java setter that does the same. What does `discountBps = 12_000` leave behind?

alt.title: Discount.java

recap: Class delegation (`: Iface by x`) forwards every interface method you don't override to `x`, captured once into a hidden final `$$delegate_0` field. Reassigning a `var` doesn't move it.
`equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` are not forwarded, and the delegate never calls back into your overrides.

A delegated property compiles to a `prop$delegate` field, a static `$$delegatedProperties` array of `KProperty` objects, and accessors that call `getValue` and `setValue`. Java sees plain getters and setters.
`by lazy` costs a `Lazy` object and an initializer lambda per instance, plus an interface call on every read. It doesn't cache exceptions. Use `NONE` for single-threaded objects.
`observable` runs after an assignment, `vetoable` before it, and `by map` reads a key named after the property when you read it.
`provideDelegate` runs once per property while the object is built: the place for early validation and registration.

quiz.q:
What does this print?

```kotlin
class Fees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy

val fees = Fees(FlatFee(25))
fees.policy = FlatFee(99)
println(fees.feeMinor(10_000))
```
options: An `IllegalStateException`
quiz.why: `by policy` reads the constructor argument once and stores it in `$$delegate_0`. The generated `feeMinor` calls that field, so the swap changes only the property. 99 is what a hand-written decorator that reads its field each call would print.

quiz.q: Which fields does `class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") }` have in the bytecode?
options: `private String status`
`private final Audited status$delegate`, plus a static `KProperty[] $$delegatedProperties`
One static `Audited` shared by every `Order`
None: the delegate is inlined into `getStatus`
quiz.why: Each delegated property gets a hidden field holding its delegate, typed as the delegate expression, and each class gets one static array of `KProperty` objects that the accessors pass to `getValue` and `setValue`. Nothing is shared between instances, and nothing is inlined.

quiz.q: An `AuthorizationEvent` is created 2 million times a minute in a Kafka consumer. It has `val summary: String by lazy { describe(this) }`, which is read for about 1% of events. What's the best change?
options: Keep it: `lazy` costs nothing until it's read
Switch to `lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION)`
Mark the property `@Volatile`
Make it a function or a getter, `val summary get() = describe(this)`, computed on demand
quiz.why: `lazy` allocates the `Lazy` object and the initializer lambda in the constructor, for every event, read or not. A getter without a backing field costs nothing until called. Changing the mode keeps both allocations; it only changes the locking.

quiz.q: `class IssuerConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val port: Int by settings }`, and `settings` has no `"port"` key. When does it fail?
options: When `IssuerConfig` is constructed
At compile time
Never: `port` reads as 0
When `port` is read: `NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map.`
quiz.why: A map-backed property is a lookup in its getter. Building the object only stores the map. To fail at construction, check the key in a `provideDelegate`, which runs while the object is built.

quiz.q: From the memory model track: two threads read `val rules by lazy { download() }` for the first time at the same moment. What happens?
options: `download()` may run twice, and each thread keeps its own result
`download()` runs once; the other thread waits and sees the same value
Nothing is guaranteed unless the property is `@Volatile`
The second thread gets `ConcurrentModificationException`
quiz.why: The default mode is `SYNCHRONIZED`: double-checked locking with a lock, so one thread runs the initializer and the other waits for it. The first option describes `PUBLICATION`, where several threads may run it but all see the first stored value.

flashcards.front: `class Fees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy`. After `fees.policy = other`, which object gets the calls?
flashcards.back: The original one. The compiler copied it into a hidden final field, `$$delegate_0`, at construction.
No. They come from `Any`, not from the interface. Override them yourself if the wrapper should behave like what it wraps.

flashcards.front: Which functions does a delegate for a `var` need?
flashcards.back: `getValue(thisRef, property: KProperty<*>)` and `setValue(thisRef, property, value)`, as operators or via `ReadWriteProperty`. A `val` needs only `getValue`.

flashcards.front: What does the compiler generate for `var status by Audited("NEW")`?
flashcards.back: A `status$delegate` field holding the delegate, a static `$$delegatedProperties` array of `KProperty`, and accessors that call `getValue`/`setValue` on the delegate.

flashcards.front: What does `by lazy` cost per instance?
flashcards.back: A `Lazy` object (`SynchronizedLazyImpl` by default) and an initializer lambda, created in the constructor, plus an interface call, and unboxing for primitives, on every read.

flashcards.front: `observable` vs `vetoable`: when does each handler run?
flashcards.back: `observable` runs after the assignment. `vetoable` runs before it, and returning `false` keeps the old value.
Once per property, while the owning object is being constructed, before any read. That makes it the place for early validation.

terms.plain: `class A(x: I) : I by x`: the compiler writes every method of `I` as a call on `x`, except the ones you override.
A property whose get and set are handed to another object with `by`.
The hidden field, such as `status$delegate`, that holds a property's delegate.
A run-time description of a property (its name, its type), passed to `getValue` and `setValue`.
The standard delegate that computes a value on first read and keeps it. Three thread-safety modes.
An operator the compiler calls once per property at construction, to create or check the real delegate.
`val host: String by settings`: reads `settings["host"]` each time the property is read.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks what the compiler actually generates for `var status: String by log.recorded("NEW")` in a class, and what a Java caller sees when it calls `setStatus`. Explain it in your own words.
explain_back.answer: `log.recorded("NEW")` returns a delegate provider, so while the object is being constructed the compiler calls its `provideDelegate` with the property's `KProperty`, and stores the `Recorded` it returns in a hidden private field called `status$delegate`. The class also gets one static array, `$$delegatedProperties`, holding a `KProperty` for each delegated property. The getter `getStatus()` loads the delegate and the matching `KProperty` and calls `getValue`, then casts the result to `String`. The setter calls `setValue(this, property, value)`, which is where `Recorded` compares the old and new value and writes a change to the log. A Java caller sees nothing special: just a public `setStatus(String)` method. It can't tell there's a delegate behind it, but the audit still happens, because the logic lives in the setter the compiler generated.
